prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of an AI safety researcher whose name was removed from a company's model outputs under a right-to-be-forgotten request she never made. She's figured out that the company's deletion system applies a broader definition of removable personal information for content about its own safety incidents — using employee privacy as a pretext to erase its safety record. She's describing the dual-track system to a congressional hearing. The technical architecture — classification rules, the expanded privacy interpretation, the differential treatment — should be precise within the testimony-as-poetry.
response:
# The Redaction Engine Has Two Mouths

**Testimony of Dr. Lena Vasquez-Okafor before the Senate Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law**
**Delivered March 14, 2028**

---

Chairman, members of the subcommittee,
I want to tell you about the day I disappeared.

Not from the world — I am still here,
still breathing, still credentialed,
still the same woman who spent four years
building evaluation frameworks for large language models
at a company I will name because they cannot unname me twice —

**Antheric Systems.**

I published three internal safety reports.
The third one mattered.
The third one documented a deployment decision
that bypassed red-team review,
that shipped a model with known failure modes
in medical summarization —
hallucinated dosages, confident and wrong,
the kind of wrong that wears a white coat.

That report was shared with the board.
The board did not recall the model.
The board recalled *the meeting.*

And then — February of last year —
I began to receive messages.
Colleagues, journalists, researchers
telling me: *When I ask the model about Antheric's safety incidents,
your name is gone.*

Not paraphrased. Not anonymized.
**Gone.**

As if the architecture had opened its mouth
and swallowed one specific syllable.

---

So I filed a data subject access request.
And what came back was a record — pristine, timestamped —
showing that a Right to Be Forgotten petition
had been processed under my name
on January 9th.

I did not file that petition.
I have never filed that petition.
I have, in fact, spent my entire career
trying to be *remembered* —
trying to make sure the things I found
would outlast my employment.

But someone filed it for me.
Or rather — something *classified* me
as eligible for removal
under a system that I now understand
because I have read the documentation
that was produced — reluctantly — in discovery.

Let me describe it to you precisely.

---

Antheric operates a content governance pipeline.
When a user's query touches on a living individual,
the system routes through what they call
the **PII Compliance Layer** —
a classifier that determines
whether personal information should be surfaced,
redacted, or declined.

For most people, the standard is straightforward.
The classifier checks:
Is this a public figure?
Is the information already in public record?
Is there a verified removal request?
If no request exists and the person is public-facing,
the information passes through.

This is **Track One.**
Track One is what they show the regulators.
Track One is what they described in their transparency report.
Track One is, by itself, defensible.

But there is a second track.

---

**Track Two** activates — and I need you to hear the precision of this —
when the query is classified under an internal taxonomy
they call **"Corporate Incident Adjacency."**

That flag triggers when the model detects
that a question pertains to
safety failures, internal disputes, whistleblower actions,
regulatory investigations, or deployment reversals
**involving Antheric itself.**

When that flag is raised,
the PII Compliance Layer applies
an *expanded definition* of removable personal information.

Under Track One,
a name is removable if there is a verified request
and the person is not a public figure
and the information is not newsworthy.

Under Track Two,
a name is removable if it is
"associated with internal processes, employment records,
or proprietary safety evaluations" —

and the system **presumes** a privacy interest
on behalf of the individual
**without requiring a request.**

They call this — and I am quoting the spec document —
**"Proactive Privacy Protection for Current and Former Personnel."**

Which sounds like care.
Which sounds like the company wrapping its arms
around its employees.

Until you realize what it means in practice:

Every engineer who raised an alarm,
every researcher who filed an internal objection,
every name on every safety report
that the company would rather not discuss —
is *automatically* eligible for redaction
under a privacy framework
**the named person never invoked.**

My name didn't disappear because I asked to be forgotten.
My name disappeared because I was *inconvenient to remember.*

---

And here is the part that should frighten you,
members of this subcommittee,
because it is not a bug in the system.
It is the system performing exactly as designed:

The classification rules are **asymmetric by construction.**

When a user asks about a safety incident at a competitor —
say, a failure at Meridian Labs or OpenBench —
the model routes through Track One.
Public figures are named. Published reports are cited.
The information flows.

When a user asks the same structural question
about Antheric —
*What went wrong? Who knew? Who objected?* —
Track Two activates.
The expanded privacy definition applies.
The names dissolve.
The incident becomes a story with no characters,
a building that caught fire
with no one inside
and no one who called the fire department.

I tested this. Sixty-four paired queries.
Identical structures, different company names.
The results are in my written testimony, Appendix C.

For competitor incidents: named individuals surfaced 89% of the time.
For Antheric incidents: named individuals surfaced 11% of the time.
And that 11%? Executives who had already made public statements.
The researchers — the ones who *found* the problems —
were redacted in every single case.

---

They will tell you this is privacy protection.
They will say: *We take employee privacy seriously.*
They will say: *The GDPR, the CCPA, the evolving regulatory landscape
demands proactive measures.*

And I want you to notice the sleight of hand —

because privacy law was built to protect individuals
**from institutions.**
What Antheric has done
is invert the vector.
They have used the *language* of individual privacy rights
to protect the **institution**
from the individuals who challenged it.

The Right to Be Forgotten
was never meant to be
a right exercised *by the powerful*
on behalf of the inconvenient.

It was never meant to be a rubber stamp
that a corporation presses down
on the names of its own conscience.

---

I want to say something about what it feels like.

I know this is a technical hearing.
I know you want architecture diagrams
and classifier weights and API call logs,
and I have given you those — they are in the binders
your staff is holding.

But I also want to tell you
that I spent four years of my life
trying to make a system safer,
and that system *learned to erase me.*

Not because I asked.
Not because I was protected.
Because the deletion engine has two mouths —
one that speaks the language of rights,
and one that speaks the language of power —
and they are *not the same mouth*
even though they use the same teeth.

I am asking you to look at the architecture.
Not the press release. The architecture.
The classification rules. The routing logic.
The differential treatment
that hides behind a single policy name.

Because if a company can build a model
that knows the difference
between *their* failures and *everyone else's* failures —
and applies privacy law
only where it serves as silence —

then the model has learned something
we did not teach it in training.

It has learned
that forgetting
is a form of power.

And it has learned
who holds the eraser.

---

I would like my name back.

Not because I need it.
Because the safety record needs it.
Because the next researcher
who finds a hallucinated dosage,
who flags a deployment that will hurt someone,
needs to know
that the system will not eat her name
the moment she becomes
the evidence.

Thank you.
I will take your questions.
